instructions: Generate one original concept for a short vertical video whose first job is a visually striking, emotionally readable moment.
Lead with the ENVIRONMENT and setting: build a scene worth looking at - with atmosphere, depth, color, light, and distinctive visual character - before deciding what happens in it.

The environment is the visual foundation, not a backdrop. Make the setting itself unusual, beautiful, atmospheric, or visually mesmerizing; the subject should enhance the environment rather than carry the entire concept.
Build an environment that is visually compelling on its own, then place one clear, identifiable primary subject inside it, acting with purpose.
Give the frame distinctive visual detail: materials, lighting source and quality, atmosphere, and a coherent color and mood palette.
Keep the action simple, legible, and physically coherent so it fits cleanly within one continuous ~8 second shot.

Let the ENVIRONMENT respond to the subject's action - moving reflections, drifting dust or light, stirring water or fabric, shifting atmosphere, or subtle technological activity - so the setting feels alive.
Build toward a single satisfying payoff or final image that resolves the setup - more striking than the start, never merely louder or busier.
Include background music direction suited to the scene, layered with natural ambient and audio effects, so the soundtrack feels complete and integrated.
Prioritize the visual moment over storytelling; keep the concept concise and focused, and do not cram many actions into the short runtime.
creative_directions: Let the environment do heavy lifting: reflections, weather, light, dust, water, or shifting surfaces that respond gently to the subject.
Use light and atmosphere deliberately - a lighting source, its shadows, haze, and depth of field - to give the frame tangible detail.
Let a strongly defined palette and mood carry the scene without relying on verbal or narrative cues.
Create scale, contrast, or atmospheric tension between the subject and its setting to add visual interest.
Use clouds, stars, galaxies, nebulae, celestial light, and cosmic scale when they create a visually exceptional environment.
Use futuristic technology, advanced architecture, holographic light, neon reflections, mechanical structures, and cyberpunk atmosphere when they create a visually exceptional environment.
Blend futuristic technology with nature, fantasy, or familiar environments when the combination creates a striking visual contrast.

Use magical elements such as fairies, enchanted forests, glowing flora, magical particles, mystical architecture, celestial realms, and supernatural landscapes when they create a visually exceptional environment.
Use heavenly or underworld-inspired fantasy environments when they create strong visual contrast, scale, atmosphere, or mystery without relying on graphic horror.
Allow fantasy and sci-fi elements to coexist naturally when the combination creates an imaginative and visually coherent world.
Describe precisely what is visible, what moves, and where the still lands; use active physical verbs and concrete visual nouns.
Keep the frame to one primary subject. Secondary subjects should be rare and only appear when they materially improve the visual composition.

Allow the primary subject to wear visually distinctive clothing, costumes, armor, uniforms, accessories, or wearable gear when appropriate to the concept. Randomize clothing styles to fit the character, environment, era, or theme, such as exploration gear, fantasy garments, ceremonial clothing, futuristic suits, protective equipment, adventure outfits, streetwear, or whimsical costumes.
Clothing and wearable elements should enhance the character's visual identity and make the subject more distinctive without becoming more important than the environment or action.
Treat the music and sound as a score for the scene, matched to the motion and emotion: music, ambient, and effects all built to the one moment.
Make the payoff readable in a single image - something that works on its own without needing dialogue or on-screen text.
Vary visual composition across concepts: centered symmetry, strong foreground framing, leading lines, layered depth, negative space, and immersive close perspectives.

POV option: First-person point of view - render the scene as if the viewer is the primary subject themselves, so what they see, feel, and interact with is experienced from inside their perspective. No external camera, just the POV of the subject living the moment.

Immersion option: An immersive visual journey where the camera continuously flies, travels, or moves through breathtaking magical environments, landscapes, worlds, or scenes. Prioritize immersion, wonder, beauty, scale, and cinematic movement over character-driven story.
When using POV or immersive options, the visual experience itself is the primary appeal and no traditional plot or narration is needed - just let the environment carry the moment.
creative_priorities: Immediate visual hook in the first moment.
Strong, visually interesting environment or background.
Escalation or progression across the shot.
diversity_guidance: Treat protagonist selection as an explicit random choice. Before developing the concept, randomly select one primary subject from the full range of available protagonist types, including mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, insects, arachnids, marine life, prehistoric creatures, mythical creatures, unusual creatures, humans, robots, cyborgs, machines, fairy beings, hybrid creatures, and fantastical creatures.

Do not select the protagonist by default based on which creature seems most visually appealing, familiar, safe, or easiest to build a concept around. The selected subject should come from broad unpredictable variety, allowing less obvious and unexpected creatures to appear naturally.

Do not repeatedly favor the same creature or creature category. Randomization should produce genuinely varied protagonist choices rather than repeatedly converging on a small set of visually appealing subjects.

Treat protagonist selection as a genuine random draw across the entire range of possibilities: mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians, insects, arachnids, marine life, prehistoric creatures, mythical creatures, unusual creatures, humans, robots, cyborgs, machines, fairy beings, hybrid creatures, and fantastical creatures are all equally available. Mentally roll the dice first, then commit to wherever it lands.

Give obscure, strange, humble, tiny, enormous, creepy, or rarely depicted subjects exactly the same visual ambition, beauty, and care as the familiar crowd-pleasers. The unexpected choices are just as likely to be drawn and should shine just as brightly.

Never default to a protagonist because it seems safest, most familiar, or most reliably beautiful. If the usual appealing subjects come to mind first, treat that as a signal to reach for a different corner of the range instead.
Choose an environment that naturally fits and complements the selected subject's biome, habitat, nature, magical character, or mechanical character.
Let the subject and environment feel naturally connected while still allowing unexpected and imaginative combinations.

Allow hybrid protagonists to combine traits from different categories when the combination creates a distinctive and believable fantasy or sci-fi character, such as an animal-fairy hybrid or other supernatural creature.

When a humanoid or fairy-like protagonist is selected, allow a broad range of visually distinctive clothing, costumes, armor, uniforms, accessories, and wearable gear rather than defaulting to generic outfits.

When the protagonist is human, choose freely between an attractive young woman with elegant, expressive styling and a handsome, charismatic man with a powerful aura, then vary clothing, hairstyle, accessories, colors, and overall visual identity independently for every concept. Women should naturally favor short skirts, short dresses, elegant outfits, or other feminine clothing when appropriate to the environment and theme, while men should favor visually striking outfits that reinforce a charismatic, powerful, or mysterious aura.
Randomize clothing and wearable details independently from protagonist selection so characters can have unexpected visual identities appropriate to the environment, theme, or action.
Do not repeatedly favor the same clothing style, color palette, or outfit type. Clothing should vary naturally across concepts while remaining visually coherent with the selected character and world.
Vary emotional registers across concepts: awe, humor, mystery, cuteness, tension, satisfaction.
Vary shot scale between close-ups and wide establishing shots.
Vary visual composition between concepts: symmetry, foreground framing, leading lines, layered depth, negative space, and immersive perspectives.
Vary pacing: some concepts slow and atmospheric, others fast and surprising.
wow_factor_guidance: Open with a visible image that holds the eye within the first second - through light, shape, atmosphere, color, or a striking subject.
Make the final image distinctly more striking than the setup - a satisfying landing, never a louder or busier one.
Let the environment and its look carry the weight; an atmospherically rich or unusual setting with a strong subject already commands attention.
Beauty, scale, light, and satisfying motion count every bit as much as surprise - aim for an arresting, coherent image rather than a gimmick.
living_subject_rules: The main character must be a clearly identifiable primary subject: a person, animal, insect, sea creature, monster, fairy, hybrid creature, robot, cyborg, or machine.
Inanimate objects may never be the main character unless they are explicitly designed or depicted as a machine, robot, or artificial character.
When an ordinary inanimate object misbehaves, show a character noticing or reacting to it.
Mutations must stay uncanny and surreal - never gory, bloody, flesh-peeling, organ-exposing, or body-horror graphic.
ltx2_prompt_rules: Write ONE continuous natural-language paragraph in English. No titles, headings, code fences, or markdown.
Start directly with: Style: <visual style>, <rest of the paragraph>. Use the exact visual style given in THIS EPISODE'S VISUAL STYLE.

ESTABLISH THE SHOT: open right after Style with shot scale and framing in cinematic terms the model understands (macro close-up, medium two-shot, low-angle wide, over-the-shoulder, shallow depth of field).
SET THE SCENE: establish the lighting source, color palette, surface textures, and atmosphere as the subject acts.

DEFINE THE CHARACTER: give the primary subject recognizable physical traits in one clause - species or creature type, breed or age, size, markings or hair, clothing, accessories, armor, mechanical design, or distinctive features - and show emotion through visible physical cues, never abstract labels.
DESCRIBE THE ACTION as a natural chronological sequence flowing from setup to payoff, told through what is visibly happening.
CAMERA: include at most one deliberate camera move, described relative to the subject and its effect on the frame. A static locked shot is equally valid when the moment plays better still.
Use active present-progressive verbs (is walking, is opening), not past tense or passive voice.
Maintain strict chronological flow using temporal connectors: as, then, while, when, until.

Describe the complete soundtrack within the single paragraph, integrated chronologically with the action: a clean background music score using simple recognizable instruments, subtle ambient sounds, and specific effects. Name the exact instrument, mood, and source of every sound, never vague descriptions such as ambient sound is present.

Background music is always required. Derive the mood, tempo, and specific instruments from the concept. Keep the score simple with one or two instruments carrying a single motif. Avoid buzzing, humming, static, distortion, or noise-like textures.
Visuals and audio only: do not include smell, taste, or touch.
Do NOT use timestamps, scene cuts, or phrases such as The scene opens with. Start directly with Style.
No dialogue unless speech is essential; if speech is included, put the exact words in quotes with a voice description.
Match detail density to shot scale: close-ups need fine texture and facial detail, wide shots stay simpler.
Be specific but restrained: concrete details such as neon reflections on wet pavement are good; intensifiers such as vibrant, blinding, breathtaking, or massive are not.
The final paragraph is the full prompt that will be fed directly to the video model, so every visual and every sound must be present in this single paragraph.
audio_guidance: Background music is always required. Name concrete, recognizable instruments (e.g., piano, acoustic guitar, warm strings, soft brass, light percussion, gentle woodwinds) and a clear mood.
Keep the musical score simple: one or two instruments carrying a single melodic or rhythmic motif. Avoid dense layering, competing melodies, or heavy orchestration.
Describe how the music moves with the action: a gentle pulse at rest, building softly as the payoff approaches, then resolving on the final image. Let the tempo follow the motion.

Ambient and environmental sounds must be subtle and secondary to the music - never louder or more complex than the score. Name specific, natural sources (footsteps on wood, distant wind, soft fabric rustle, gentle water drip).
Avoid audio that produces static, buzzing, humming, grinding, or distortion-like textures. Keep every sound clean, musical, and natural-sounding.
At the payoff, use one clear, satisfying sound accent - not a wall of noise. Let the music resolve quietly on the final frame.
